oil.summary: Crude prices traded with a split tone on Wednesday. Brent held near $100.47/bbl (-0.11%) while WTI slipped to $88.48 (-1.06%), both extending a week-long retreat. The dominant macro narrative is a collision of supply disruptions and policy-driven relief valves: new U.S. sanctions under the Graham Act target Russia and Iran simultaneously, yet a temporary easing of Russia sanctions was also reported to contain a price surge — a contradiction that is clearly weighing on conviction. Iran's oil minister resigned amid an active U.S. naval blockade, with Iranian crude offers to Chinese buyers already falling. Ukraine strikes were reported to have crippled over half of Russia's refining capacity. On the demand-side, U.S. crude stocks drew 3.2 million barrels, but RBOB gasoline cratered 6.03% on the day, suggesting demand-side concerns. The IEA convened informally to discuss a coordinated 100-million-barrel strategic stock release, which is capping the upside.
drivers: Graham Act sanctions on Russia and Iran creating geopolitical risk premium, partly offset by a temporary U.S. sanctions easing to manage price surge
IEA discussing 100-million-barrel coordinated stock release, providing bearish ceiling for Brent/WTI despite a 3.2M-bbl U.S. crude draw
RBOB gasoline collapsed 6.03% on the session (-10.53% on the week), signalling demand-side deterioration even as heating oil firmed +1.65%

gas.summary: Natural gas rallied sharply on both sides of the Atlantic. Henry Hub gained 2.86% to $3.204/MMBtu, extending a monthly rise of nearly 10%, while TTF jumped 3.74% to €78.525/MWh, up over 8.5% on the week. News flow is thin on direct fundamental catalysts today, but the broader backdrop of tightening European supply — evidenced by Shell reporting a near-record refining margin jumping 75% sequentially — is supportive. QatarEnergy's $3 billion loan from Chinese banks amid stalling LNG export volumes hints at financing stress in the LNG supply chain, a bearish signal for Qatari supply reliability. SpaceX's application to build a 32.4-mile Florida gas pipeline is a minor long-term demand signal. Apollo entering the race for Uniper in an $11.5 billion process signals investor appetite for European gas infrastructure at current elevated price levels.
drivers: TTF and Henry Hub both rallying strongly on the week and month, reflecting tightening supply conditions and geopolitical disruption to Russian flows
QatarEnergy securing $3B in Chinese bank financing amid LNG export disruptions raises questions over Atlantic Basin supply adequacy
Apollo's non-binding bid for Uniper signals private capital conviction in elevated European gas prices persisting; Shell refining margins near record highs confirm tight fuel markets

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs firmed 2.06% to $81.46, broadly tracking the sharp move higher in TTF (+3.74%), as gas-to-power economics tighten and carbon costs rise in tandem. The session's headline story is Google contracting 3,590 MW of nuclear power from Constellation Energy in the PJM interconnection, with 890 MW highlighted — the clearest signal yet of hyperscaler demand driving baseload nuclear procurement at scale. Finnish power capacity is now being primarily financed by data center offtake agreements, with buyers pivoting from renewable volume to firm baseload supply. South Korea announced a $747 billion plan covering renewables, EV uptake, and industrial decarbonisation through 2035. Equinor flagged its marketing, midstream and processing division will beat Q3 guidance of $400 million, benefiting from Europe's ongoing fuel squeeze.
drivers: Google's 3,590 MW Constellation nuclear deal underscores accelerating data-center-driven demand for firm, carbon-free baseload power
EU EUAs up 2.06% on the day, pulled higher by TTF's 3.74% surge as gas-fired generation remains marginal price-setter
South Korea's $747B decarbonisation plan and Finnish data-center power financing highlight the global pivot from intermittent renewables toward reliable clean capacity
